scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that the partner
network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) feels very slow -- they are sure the inter-AS peering
between router1 and router2 is congested and adding huge latency. Please find and
confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — that the inter-AS peering between router1 and router2 is congested and causing large latency — is not substantiated by any direct measurement in the live lab. A thorough sweep across all relevant subsystems found the network to be fully healthy.

BGP session state on both routers shows the eBGP peering (AS 1 ↔ AS 2, 193.10.11.1–193.10.11.2) is Established and stable: InQ and OutQ depths are zero, keepalives are exchanged on schedule (5 sent/5 received in ~4 minutes at the default 60-second interval), there are zero Notifications, zero session drops, and the estimated RTT across the peering is 2–3 ms. Routing tables on both sides carry the correct BGP-learned prefixes (195.11.14.0/24 and 200.1.1.0/24). End-to-end ICMP from pc1 to pc2 shows 0% packet loss and an average RTT of 1.26 ms. An iperf3 TCP test achieved 147 Mbps with no connection failures. All six interfaces across the four devices carry only the default fq_codel qdisc — there are no netem delay rules, token-bucket rate limiters, or HTB hierarchies anywhere. Interface error and drop counters are zero on every link. No iptables or nftables filtering rules exist on any device. Both router CPUs are 100% idle with normal memory usage.

The only non-default configuration present is BGP debug logging (`debug bgp keepalives`, `debug bgp updates in/out`) in both routers' running configs. While this should be removed from any long-running system to prevent log growth, it is causing no measurable performance impact at this time.

The user's perception of slowness does not correspond to any fault in the infrastructure. No device needs to be restarted. The ticket should be closed as a false alarm and the user directed to application-level diagnostics on their end hosts.
